newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai party seen trying to form cleaner coalition.
newsitem.headline: Thai party seen trying to form cleaner coalition.

text.p: The victorious New Aspiration Party's (NAP) move to change coalition partners was a bid to improve a future Thai government's image, but uncertainty is still seen in the near-term, analysts said on Monday.

The NAP, which won a two-seat victory in Sunday's general election over its arch-rival the Democrat Party, said on Monday it agreed to form a six-party coalition which would have a comfortable majority of 221 seats in the 393-seat parliament.
The coalition comprises the NAP, Chart Pattana, Social Action Party, Prachakorn Thai, Seritham and Muon Chon parties.

Previously, NAP leader Chavalit Yongchaiyudh had been talking about linking up with four parties, including the Chart Thai party led by caretaker prime minister Banharn Silpa-archa. That group did not include Chart Pattana, led by charismatic former premier Chatichai Choonhavan, who was deposed in a bloodless coup in 1991 after two and a half years in power.

Analysts said the decision to include Chart Pattana instead of Chart Thai was to try to avoid image problems -- especially because Chatichai's party was not in the previous administration, which was widely accused of corruption and mismanagement.
"Chart Pattana MPs are relatively better in terms of image. That's why NAP is bringing in Chart Pattana instead of Chart Thai," said Arporn Chewakrengkai, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The first group of five parties talking of forming a coalition were all members of Banharn's government, which analysts said was a mark against the coalition from the start.
Of the present group of six, the NAP, Social Action, Muon Chon and Prachakorn Thai were part of Banharn's coalition.
Banharn's chaotic administration was blamed for many of Thailand's economic problems, including sagging exports, a widening current account deficit and a stock market that is near three-year lows.
The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) took a six percent dive at the open on Monday on news of the NAP victory and the likely makeup of the coalition, brokers and analysts said.
News of the group of coalition partners shortly after the midday break helped lift prices slightly, but they were still down nearly six percent at the close.
Analysts said uncertainty in the market is likely to continue as coalition partners wrangle over portfolios.
Before the election, dubbed the dirtiest and most violent in decades, the business community had pinned its hopes on a Democrat victory because of the Democrat's strong economic team.
Chart Pattana has stronger economic candidates than Chart Thai, but the coalition was likely to rely mostly on outside experts to take key economic portfolios, analysts said.
But until the makeup of the cabinet was announced, the market was likely to remain unstable, they said.

"These developments spell rough times ahead for the SET as investors wait for the dust to settle," Seamico Securities said in a report. "As the NAP struggles to put together its team, rumours will fuel market movements."
Chavalit has vowed to form a cabinet that would be acceptable to the public.

A new government is not expected to be sworn in for about two weeks. King Bhumibol Adulyadej must first issue a royal decree setting a date for parliament to reconvene. Then a speaker must be chosen who will then forward the nomination of a prime minister -- most likely Chavalit -- to the king for approval.
After the premier is approved, he will then submit a list of cabinet members for royal approval.
There is no set deadline for the procedures to take place but it is usually within a week or two of the election, political analysts said.
